newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: TSUMEB STRIKE SEEN COSTING N$50-100 MLN.
newsitem.headline: TSUMEB STRIKE SEEN COSTING N$50-100 MLN.

text.p: The bitter six-week strike at Tsumeb Corp Ltd, which this weekend reached a settlement after a week of violent protest, is estimated to have cost N$50-100 million, owners Goldfields of Namibia Ltd said Monday.
"We have put out a figure of between N$50-100 million," a Goldfields spokesman told Reuters by telephone from Namibia.
Earlier Tsumeb (TCL) said it had agreed with the Mineworkers Union of Nambia (MUN) for a 10.5 percent wage increase after a mediation process that was brokered by the Namibian government.
The agreement, reached on Saturday, ends the pay dispute which exploded into crisis last week after armed MUN members took control of the group's three copper mines -- Otjihase, Kombat and Tsumeb.
The company is now back in control of the mines, but the process of repairing damaged workings and getting the copper smelter running again will take some time.
Gold Fields said that the Otjihase Mine was flooding and water from the old mine at Tsumeb, which supplies the town, is threatened with contamination.
"We will try and get the copper smelter up and running chop-chop, but that doesn't mean one week. It will take more like eight weeks," the spokesman said.
The news of the agreement boosted Goldfields Namibia's share price and by 1355 GMT it had gained 18 cents to stand at 150 cents on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.
"If that strike gets resolved properly there is a lot of potential recovery there," said one analyst who declined to be named.

Analysts said the assets of the group were of a high quality, but warned that the legacy of the strike -- which at one stage saw mine manager Tony de Beer blockaded in his house for two days -- had damaged market confidence in its management.
"When you get that sort of strike it always puts a question mark over the management's handling of it," said one analyst.

The Goldfields spokesman said the firm's main priorites were to turn Tsumeb into a profitable firm once again and set about implementing the agreement. Internal inquiries into the strike's handling and why it started may come later, he added.
"We have go to implement the agreement first...we have to go forward and make Tsumeb a profitable company," he said.
But he warned that the settlement, which includes retrenchments, could damage morale as workers lose their jobs.
